text: A QRS duration of at least 120 ms supports a ventricular conduction disturbance.
A PR interval of at least 200 ms supports delayed atrioventricular conduction.
A frontal QRS axis at or below -30 degrees supports left axis deviation.
Sokolow-Lyon voltage, the absolute S-wave amplitude in V1 plus the larger R-wave amplitude in V5 or V6, of at least 3.5 mV supports left ventricular hypertrophy.
A Bazett-corrected QT of at least 450 ms in men or 460 ms in women supports delayed ventricular repolarization.
An ST amplitude of -0.1 mV or lower in lead II supports ST-segment depression.
A Q wave lasting at least 40 ms in lead II, III, aVF, or V1 through V4 supports a prior infarct pattern.
A ventricular rate of at least 100 beats per minute is a tachycardia-range rate. Rate alone does not establish a diagnostic superclass.
A QRS duration under 110 ms supports a narrow QRS and argues against a complete bundle-branch block.
A PR interval under 120 ms is a short PR. It is not evidence of delayed atrioventricular conduction.
A frontal QRS axis of at least 90 degrees supports right axis deviation.
Sokolow-Lyon voltage below 3.5 mV does not meet the voltage threshold used here for left ventricular hypertrophy.
A ventricular rate under 60 beats per minute is a bradycardia-range rate. Rate alone does not establish a diagnostic superclass.
An ST amplitude of at least 0.1 mV in lead II supports ST-segment elevation in that lead.
A 1 mV calibration pulse checks the recorder gain. It is not a finding about this patient.
A paper speed of 25 mm/s is a display choice and does not support a diagnosis.
A 50 Hz or 60 Hz notch filter is an acquisition setting, not a conduction abnormality.
QRS duration cutoffs used for infants do not apply as adult bundle-branch criteria.
A story about swapped limb leads is not a measurement of the frontal QRS axis.
Older age raises the chance of prior infarction, but age is not a Q-wave measurement.
A blood troponin result is not contained in this ECG and cannot be read from the tracing.
Wall thickness on an echocardiogram is not an ECG voltage measurement.
A serum potassium value is not an ST-segment measurement.
Digoxin can be associated with ST change, but medication history is not in this ECG.
Hyperventilation can change ST segments. A respiratory story is not an ST measurement.
Using the male QT cutoff for a woman, or the reverse, is not the sex-specific rule.
Seeing a Q wave without measuring its duration is not the 40 ms Q-wave rule.
Naming early repolarization does not establish an ST measurement.
A pacing spike is not the same measurement as a QRS duration of 120 ms.
A changing sinus rate is not evidence of infarction, hypertrophy, or a conduction block.
An upright T wave in lead II does not establish ST-segment depression.
A tall R wave in V1 alone is not the Sokolow-Lyon sum of V1 and V5 or V6.
Poor R-wave progression is a descriptive phrase and is not the 40 ms Q-wave rule.
A broad P wave is not a ventricular voltage criterion.
A U wave is not an ST-segment measurement.
Naming the J point does not establish ST depression of 0.1 mV.
An epsilon wave is not the same finding as a QRS duration of 120 ms.
A capture beat is a rhythm event, not a PR-interval measurement.
A fusion beat is not, by itself, delayed atrioventricular conduction.
Electrical alternans is a beat-to-beat amplitude pattern, not the Sokolow-Lyon voltage.
A clinical story of pericarditis is not an ST measurement from lead II.
Naming dextrocardia is not the same as measuring a frontal axis at or below -30 degrees.
Athletic training can increase voltage. Training status is not in this ECG.
Body habitus can lower voltage. Weight is not a substitute for the measured amplitudes.
Fever can raise heart rate. It is not a measurement of the QRS.
Caffeine intake is not an ECG measurement.
The printed grid on ECG paper is not a patient measurement.
